Irish whiskey producers are changing course to combat challenges in the US *This feature was originally published in the September 2026 issue of The Spirits Business magazine. In 2008, US sales of Irish whiskey were just over a million cases , according to the Distilled Spirits Council of the US (Discus). At the time there were just four operating distilleries in Ireland dominated as ever, by Midleton in County Cork, home to Pernod Ricard’s power brand – Jameson. From then, the number of distilleries exploded to almost 50, while US sales soared to 6.1m cases with a value of US$1.4 billion in 2022 (Discus data). “We were making hay while the sun shines. At one stage I could sell every drop of whiskey two or three times over,” says John Teeling, chairman and co-founder of the Great Northern Distillery, about those heady days. With a production capacity of 8m litres per annum of malt whiskey and 12m of grain, Great Northern has been the country’s go-to source of new make spirit, fuelling the boom in new brands, while helping some of the big players keep up with demand. After the party, came the hangover. It still lingers in the US, which consumes around one in three bottles of Irish whiskey or more than six times any other market. Last year, US sales were down to 4.5m cases (from 4.8m in 2024), Discus data showed. “When the US gets a cold, Great Northern gets pneumonia,” says Teeling, who dates the fallout to early 2024 when the extent of overstocking in the market became clear. “That recession was predicted to last 18 months, but then the tariffs came in, causing more uncertainty, and there was huge front-end loading again, and that further screwed up the ratios of inventory to sales at retail,” he says. Other factors include the wave of speculators who piled in and have since vanished, and the recent failure of Republic National Distributing Company (RNDC) – the big US wholesaler that many smaller brands were using. During the period, he reckons Jameson’s was “more-or-less flat [in the US] which means others have suffered much worse”. But the brand was not immune from the fall-out. In April 2025 Pernod paused production at its giant Midleton whiskey site for three months, and delayed completion of a €250m (US$291m) expansion until at least 2027. Peter Mulryan, founder and CEO of Waterford’s Blackwater distillery believes the overall market “is beginning to stabilise, but there is still a lot of downward pressure”. He points to the collapse in new make spirit sales, and says: “That’s worrying because that’s the real future. That’s not about people investing in Capex and bricks and mortar. It’s about brands investing, and they’re not.” There has been good news with the recent rescue of three shuttered distilleries; Powerscourt, now back in production, Waterford, which was bought from the receivers by Tennessee Distilling Group in March, and Killarney, which was acquired by Swiss equity firm Spirit Capital in July. A complete steal However, Mulryan points to the prices paid, and says: “I think Killarney was a couple of million euros – that was a complete steal. If something’s low enough, it will sell.” John Cashman, head of brand and new product development at Powerscourt, has no doubt the category will rebound. “It’s inevitable,” he says. “Whether it has started yet, I’m not 100% sure. You’re seeing a lot of companies moving away from traditional Irish whiskey markets and finding growth in other markets. For example, Nigeria will become our largest market this year, and China has been very good for us.” This year, Powerscourt, nestled in the beautiful Wicklow hills south of Dublin, was rescued by US private investment firm Altiva Management. It had gone into receivership in June 2025 after an apparent falling out among its previous owners. Whatever its issues “it had nothing to do with the quality of Fercullen”, says Cashman of its award-winning whiskey. “We were too good to fail.” That may be the fate of others caught in the backwash from the US, but in his view: “Those with an authentic story, a good brand and their own source of liquid are the ones that are probably going to survive.” High visibility: the still at Great Northern Distillery The other key ingredient is having the right importer or agent. “We have a very good partner in Nigeria, focusing on the on-trade, doing lots of activations and investing in celebrity endorsements,” Cashman says. Mulryan adds: “The US was never a huge market for us. We quickly learnt our lesson. We went into a couple of States and pulled out, and now focus exclusively on the EU.” Whether the nearby Waterford distillery will focus on the US remains to be seen. Production has yet to restart, and its new owners are “keeping their powder very dry” says Mulyran. Tennessee Distilling’s business model is in contract distilling. At Royal Oak in Carlow, the focus is entirely on The Busker and its flagship ‘Triple Cask Triple Smooth’ blend that is matured in Bourbon, sherry, and Marsala casks. The distillery began as a joint venture with Italy’s Disaronno Group which took full ownership in 2019, launching The Busker a year later during the Covid-19 pandemic. Alan Dempsey, general manager and brown spirits lead, is glad about having Italian parents. “What we’re very grateful for is being backed by a drinks company and not an investment bank, who understood the need to fund the distillery through these difficult times,” he says. “Things are quite turbulent at the moment. Having Disaronno gives us insulation from the craziness out there.” Royal Oak has had to cut production by 20%, but its brand is doing surprisingly well in a market it was never intended for. The Busker was aimed at the West, but it has really taken off in Japan, to the extent it is now the number-one Irish whiskey there. “In a Highball, the liquid stands up, and just works really well,” says Dempsey. For Ffion FitzGerald, Disaronno’s global brand director brown spirits: “It’s an interesting lesson when you launch a new brand to be open to seeing where it resonates, and not being hell-bent on the original plan.” She puts its Japanese success down to building “a great reputation with bartenders, targeting those high-energy, sociable moments of connection, and we’ve looked to introduce new entry points into the brand” such as ready-to-drink (RTD). For Dempsey there was also an element of luck. “We just happened to be in Asia when everyone was looking at the US,” he says. The question now is how to replicate that success in other markets. With 10 years of aged stocks at Royal Oak, FitzGerald believes there is “huge headroom for premiumisation, and space to offer something new in super-premium whiskeys”. The Busker also comes as a single grain, a single malt, and a pot still Irish whiskey. The Busker did try to make it in the US, as did Kinahan’s, a legacy brand founded in 1779 that was relaunched in 2014 by Zak Oganian, CEO of Origen X. Within two or three years he says he realised the US “was overheated in every respect. You had importers suddenly saying ‘we’re importers not brand builders’, and distributors saying ‘we’re distributors, not your sales team’, so everything was shoved back to the brand owner.” Today, Kinahan’s is in 45 markets In 2016, Kinahan’s began to pivot towards Europe and Asia, and is today in 45 markets with not a drop in the US. Poland is Irish whiskey’s second-biggest market, with sales of around 700,000 cases. For Oganian it is “way ahead of other East European markets in terms of consumer willingness to explore the category and buy new brands”. However, he admits that Polish retail is becoming somewhat saturated with freshly minted Irish labels that come and go. As for China, called a market of “monumental potential” by the Irish Whiskey Association, Oganian’s advice is “find one good regional importer and stick there. A ‘small’ retail chain there can have 3,000 stores, and no-one knows about it.” This summer, John Teeling signed a partnership with the giant Chinese brewer Tsingtao, and, at the time of writing, two containers of Great Northern whiskey were already on the way there. The shipment includes “a 12-year-old for nightclubs and high-end hotels and bars, and a five-year-old for more general distribution”, he explains. His sons, Jack and Stephen, are still involved with their Teeling distillery in Dublin, which was fully acquired by Bacardi in June. As they become more involved with Great Northern, the pressure to produce brands rather than the bulk whiskey beloved by their father will doubtless increase. “They’re purely brand guys,” says John Teeling. “I’m like John Wayne at the Alamo. I’m 80 and I’m fighting to the end.” For now, what excites him the most is India, where Irish whiskey is “on an early-adopter curve”, he says. “Jameson had been there for 15 years, struggling along the bottom and then it took off. Jameson will sell over 1m cases this year in India. There’s a very good chance India will be the biggest market for Irish whiskey within 10 years.” Industry insights What do you think will define the next chapter of Irish whiskey? Yury Surin – global marketing director, Stoli Group “Ireland has spent two decades building capacity, stock and expertise, yet for most drinkers the category is still two or three big names. Behind them stands a generation of whiskey worthy of Scotland’s great houses. Brown spirits are under pressure as drinking habits and generations shift; too many answer with discounting, which tightens the squeeze on producers, while Scotland sits on vast stocks against slowing sales. The next chapter belongs to bold experimentation, honest communication, quality over volume, and to Irish producers educating drinkers together – so Irish single malts, blends and single pot still stand alongside the great Scotch names.” Related news Irish whiskey distilleries draw 1m visitors again Midleton Very Rare Irish Chestnut Edition is first for whiskey Top 10 award-winning Irish whiskeys Most read Auberon heads to Savage Garden for Day of the Dead New bar June Baby celebrates Filipino-American culture Desi Daru celebrates Diwali in Leeds Events WBWE – World Bulk Wine Exhibition - Amesterdam November 30, 2026 - December 1, 2026 Wine Paris 2027 Porte de Versailles - Paris February 15, 2027 - February 17, 2027 More events It looks like you're in Asia, would you like to be redirected to the Drinks Business Asia edition?
